promptText: A team says they practice 'CI/CD' but every production deployment still requires a person to click 'approve' after staging tests pass. According to the distinction between Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment, which term actually describes what this team is doing when releasing to production?
options: Continuous Deployment, because the pipeline builds and tests automatically
Continuous Delivery, because every good build is auto-promoted to staging and kept releasable but a human still approves the production release
Continuous Integration, because a human is involved at some point
This isn't CI/CD at all, since any manual step anywhere disqualifies the whole process
explanation: Continuous Delivery means the pipeline keeps every build in a releasable state and auto-promotes it through staging, but a human still clicks deploy to production; Continuous Deployment removes that click entirely. Most companies claiming 'CI/CD' are actually doing continuous delivery, which is worth naming explicitly rather than treating the terms as interchangeable.

promptText: A production-grade pipeline runs static analysis/lint, unit tests, artifact build, dependency/SAST scans, and integration tests. What ordering principle should determine which of these runs first?
options: Run the most business-critical checks first regardless of how long they take
Run checks in alphabetical order of tool name for consistency
Run cheap, fast checks that are likely to catch common mistakes first, and push slow, expensive checks later
Run whichever check the CI provider executes fastest on its own infrastructure, regardless of what it tests
explanation: The pipeline is designed so failures are caught as early and cheaply as possible; a pipeline that runs a 20-minute integration suite before a 10-second lint check wastes everyone's time on every red build a trivial check would have caught first.

promptText: A team's build passed on Friday and failed on Monday even though no code changes were merged over the weekend. Which practice, if it had been followed, would most directly have prevented this?
options: Increasing the unit test coverage threshold
Pinning dependency versions and base image tags instead of using floating ranges or `latest`
Adding more parallel stages to the pipeline
Switching from scripted to declarative Jenkins pipeline syntax
explanation: A reproducible build pins everything that can silently drift -- dependency versions, base image tags, build tool versions -- because an unpinned floating range or a `latest` base image can pull in a new version overnight and break a previously passing build with zero code changes.

promptText: Why do most teams default to declarative Jenkins pipeline syntax over scripted pipelines, and what is the escape hatch when scripted-style logic is genuinely needed?
options: Declarative pipelines are always faster to execute, and scripted pipelines cannot be used once declarative is chosen
Declarative offers readability, easier review, and built-in structure validation, but you can still drop into a `script {}` block inside it for real Groovy logic
Scripted pipelines are deprecated by Jenkins and no longer supported at all
Declarative pipelines cannot call shared libraries, so scripted syntax is required for any reuse
explanation: Declarative pipelines trade some flexibility for a fixed, lintable, easy-to-review structure, but a declarative pipeline can embed a `script {}` step to drop into raw Groovy when it needs loops or custom logic -- the choice is not all-or-nothing for the whole file.

promptText: In a GitHub Actions workflow with two jobs, `build` and `deploy`, that have no explicit `needs:` relationship declared between them, how will they execute?
options: Sequentially, in the order they're listed in the YAML file
In parallel and isolated on separate runners, since jobs run in parallel by default unless a dependency is declared
`deploy` will automatically wait for `build` simply because it appears later in the file
The workflow will fail, because GitHub Actions requires every job to declare an explicit `needs:` relationship
explanation: GitHub Actions jobs run in parallel by default on isolated runners; an explicit dependency such as `needs: [build]` is required to make one job wait for another, mirroring GitLab's `needs:` DAG keyword.

promptText: A team's pipeline is green on every single run, yet the chapter argues this alone doesn't prove a healthy delivery process. Which set of metrics is designed to reveal the fuller picture beyond pipeline health?
options: Code coverage percentage, lines of code, and cyclomatic complexity
The four DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and mean time to restore
Number of pipeline stages and average stage count per repository
Number of GitHub stars and open issues on the repository
explanation: A pipeline can pass on every run while still representing a slow, risky delivery process; DORA metrics measure the actual delivery outcomes -- how often you ship, how fast a commit reaches production, how often a deploy causes an incident, and how fast you recover -- which a green build alone does not capture.

promptText: A backend team deploys to production multiple times a day using an automated pipeline. Why would trunk-based development typically be favored over GitFlow for this team, beyond simply being 'more modern'?
options: GitFlow is incompatible with Git and only works with older version control systems
Trunk-based development requires no code review at all, which speeds up releases
GitFlow's long-lived branches delay integration pain instead of removing it and accumulate drift that fights against a fast, continuously validating pipeline
GitFlow does not support automated testing, so it cannot be used with CI/CD at all
explanation: GitFlow's long-lived develop/release/feature branches fit slower release trains needing parallel version maintenance, but for a team deploying continuously those branches accumulate drift and postpone integration conflicts; trunk-based development's small, frequent commits to main keep merge conflicts small and keep the pipeline validating something close to what's about to ship.

promptText: Why does the 'build once, promote everywhere' principle call for promoting the exact same versioned artifact from staging to production, rather than rebuilding from source at each environment stage?
options: Rebuilding is always slower than promoting, so it is purely a speed optimization
Rebuilding at each stage risks producing a functionally different artifact than the one that was tested, due to things like dependency resolution drift or a different base image patch level
Artifact registries like Artifactory or Nexus cannot store more than one build per day
Rebuilding voids the semantic version tag, which makes rollback impossible
explanation: If each environment rebuilds from source, a different dependency version, base image patch level, or even a flaky test outcome could produce an artifact that differs from the one actually validated in staging -- promoting the identical immutable artifact guarantees what was tested is what ships.

promptText: A Jenkins setup uses long-lived static VM agents that engineers occasionally SSH into to install extra tooling by hand. What criticism does the chapter raise about this approach, and what is the recommended alternative?
options: Static agents are criticized only for cost; the fix is to reduce the number of executors per agent
Static agents accumulate configuration drift and 'works on this specific box' problems; ephemeral, containerized agents (e.g. via the Kubernetes plugin, spinning up a fresh pod per build) avoid this
Static agents are fine as long as they use node labels; the criticism only applies to agents without labels
The controller should run the builds itself instead of delegating to any agents
explanation: Long-lived static agents drift out of sync with each other over time as ad hoc changes accumulate, recreating exactly the 'works on this machine' problem Docker was meant to solve; ephemeral containerized agents provision a clean, identical environment for every single build.

promptText: A platform team wants every service repository's entire CI pipeline to literally be 'call our standard workflow,' including defining its own jobs, inputs, secrets, and runner choice. Which GitHub Actions reuse mechanism fits this, and why not the alternative?
options: A composite action, because composite actions can define their own jobs and choose their own runner

A reusable workflow, because it is a whole separate workflow file with its own jobs and runner choice invoked via `uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1`; a composite action only bundles steps that run within the calling job's own runner
Either works identically, since both operate at the same scope in GitHub Actions
Neither; GitHub Actions has no mechanism for cross-repository pipeline reuse, unlike GitLab's `include:`
explanation: A composite action de-duplicates a handful of steps and always executes inside the caller's own job and runner context, while a reusable workflow is a full standalone workflow with its own jobs, inputs, secrets, and runner selection -- the right fit when you want to centralize an entire pipeline, not just a step sequence.

promptText: A team configures its CI pipeline to pass the compiled jar from the build job to the deploy job using a dependency cache keyed on the pom.xml hash, instead of an explicit artifact upload/download. What is the risk in this design?
options: There is no risk; cache and artifact are interchangeable mechanisms for passing files between jobs

A cache is a best-effort speed optimization that can be silently missing or stale, whereas an artifact is a guaranteed, explicit hand-off -- using a cache where an artifact was needed is a classic subtle CI bug
Caches are always slower than artifacts, so this only costs pipeline time, never correctness
Caches cannot be restored across different jobs within the same workflow run, so the deploy job would immediately fail
explanation: A cache exists purely to speed up rebuilds and its presence is never guaranteed -- a cache miss or eviction could leave the deploy job with a stale or missing jar -- while an artifact is an explicit, reliable hand-off between jobs; conflating the two is a real and subtle source of pipeline bugs.

promptText: Why does exchanging a CI-issued OIDC token for temporary cloud credentials reduce security risk compared to storing a static AWS access key as a pipeline secret?
options: OIDC tokens use a stronger encryption algorithm than static keys, making them mathematically harder to brute-force

There is no long-lived secret to leak in the first place -- the exchanged credential is scoped narrowly and expires within the hour, shrinking blast radius compared to a static key that sits in secrets until someone remembers to rotate it
OIDC eliminates the need for any IAM role configuration on the cloud provider side
OIDC tokens are stored in the same secrets store as static keys, so the benefit is purely organizational, not technical
explanation: A static cloud key persists indefinitely as a high-value target until manually rotated; OIDC has the cloud provider trust the CI issuer and mint a short-lived, narrowly-scoped credential per job run, so even a compromised action or leaked log entry exposes only a credential that expires shortly and does little damage.

promptText: A Jenkinsfile injects a production database password via `credentials('prod-db-password')`, relying on Jenkins's automatic console-log masking to keep it safe. A script inside that step deliberately writes the password to a debug file instead of stdout. What does this scenario illustrate about credential handling in Jenkins, and what mitigates it?
options: This is impossible, because Jenkins encrypts every file written during a build, not just console output

Masking only redacts values Jenkins recognizes in console output -- it does not stop a script from deliberately writing or reformatting a credential elsewhere -- so least-privilege scoping of the credential (e.g. folder-level rather than global) matters as much as masking
The fix is to switch to a scripted pipeline, since declarative pipelines cannot mask credentials at all
This can only happen if the credential is stored as 'Secret text' rather than 'Username and password'
explanation: Log masking is a console-output filter, not encryption of everything the build touches -- a script that writes a credential to a file or pipes it through a reformatting tool can still leak it, so limiting which jobs or folders can even access a given credential (least privilege) is the layer of defense masking cannot provide.

promptText: A team enforces 'fail the build if line coverage drops below 80%' as a hard gate. Developers respond by writing tests that execute lines without asserting meaningful behavior, just to hit the number. Which combination of changes would most directly address this without abandoning coverage as a signal entirely?
options: Raise the threshold to 95% so gaming the number becomes harder
Remove the coverage gate entirely, since any coverage requirement inevitably gets gamed

Gate on diff coverage for new/changed lines rather than a global percentage, treat the overall number as a trend rather than a pass/fail cliff, and occasionally run mutation testing to catch assertion-free 'coverage theatre' that line coverage cannot detect
Switch from a line-coverage tool to a branch-coverage tool, which cannot be gamed the same way
explanation: Line coverage only measures which lines executed, never whether the logic was correctly asserted on, so raising the threshold just raises the bar for gaming it; gating on diff coverage focuses pressure on the actual change, and mutation testing (e.g. PIT) specifically catches tests that run code without meaningfully verifying its behavior.

promptText: A team plans to rename a database column in a single deploy: they'll run `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` and ship application code that reads/writes the new name in the same pipeline run, using a rolling deployment strategy. What two problems from the chapter's guidance does this plan combine, and what is the safer approach?
options: There's no real problem as long as the migration runs before the application code deploys in the same pipeline
The only risk is that the rename might be slow; running it during off-peak hours fully resolves it

During a rolling deploy, old and new app versions run against the schema simultaneously, so a single-step rename breaks the old version reading the new schema; an irreversible, blocking DDL statement also risks locking a large table mid-rollout. The safer approach splits it into add-new-column/dual-write/backfill, then switch reads, then drop the old column only later
Splitting the migration into multiple deploys is unnecessary as long as the migration is wrapped in a database transaction
explanation: Because a rolling or canary deploy runs old and new application code against the same schema at the same time, any migration must stay backward compatible with the previous app version -- a same-deploy rename violates that -- and running a blocking, irreversible DDL statement inside the deploy step risks locking a large table and taking the service down, which is why the chapter recommends multi-step expand/contract migrations as their own gated step, ideally with an online-schema-change tool for large tables.
